conceptTag: Should a bakery take a big wholesale order?
readerTitle: Should the bakery take the supermarket order?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (동네 빵집과 지역 슈퍼마켓 체인, 소형 배송업체) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 대량 주문은 한 덩어리로 판단하지 않는다. 남는 설비로 만드는 몫과 설비를 늘려야 하는 몫을 나눠 각각의 한계비용과 비교한다.
misconception: 주문 가격이 고정비까지 나눠 넣은 '단위 원가'보다 낮으면 손해다. 또는 재료비보다만 높으면 물량이 얼마든 이익이다.

sources.text: 미시경제학·관리회계의 표준 개념 (고정비·변동비 구분, 한계비용, 생산능력과 계단식 비용)

factChecks.note: 빵집 기본 수치: 매장 판매 하루 300개 × $6, 개당 변동비(재료·포장) $1.50, 하루 고정비 $1,200. 고정비 배분 원가 = $1.50 + $1,200 ÷ 300 = $1.50 + $4.00 = $5.50. 정규 근무 시간의 오븐 생산능력 하루 400개.
배송 사례: 회계상 배분 원가 회당 $180, 귀로 화물의 추가 비용 약 $15(적재 시간·연료) → $60 − $15 = $45 남음. 전용 운행의 추가 비용 약 $120(기사 시간·연료) → $60 − $120 = −$60. 모두 설명용 가정.

cards.title: Should the bakery take the supermarket order?
body: Mina's bakery sells 300 loaves a day at $6. A regional supermarket chain calls: they want 200 loaves a day, every day, at $3.50 each.
Her spreadsheet says each loaf costs her $5.50 to make. On paper, the offer loses money. The real answer is less simple, and it splits right down the middle of the order.

image.label: A baker holding a phone next to a rack of loaves
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작은 빵집 주방에서 제빵사가 전화를 받고 있고, 옆 선반에 빵이 가득. 말풍선에 "200 loaves a day at $3.50?". 실제 슈퍼마켓 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What should Mina say?
body: Ingredients and packaging cost $1.50 a loaf. Rent, the oven and her bakers' regular shifts cost $1,200 a day, whatever she bakes.
In a normal shift her oven can bake 400 loaves. She already bakes 300 for the shop.

options.text: No. $3.50 is below her $5.50 cost per loaf
options.feedback: The $5.50 includes rent and wages she pays anyway. Turning the order down keeps the spreadsheet tidy but leaves real money on the table.

options.text: Yes, all 200. $3.50 is well above the $1.50 in ingredients
options.feedback: Right for the first 100 loaves. But the oven only has room for 100 more, so the rest bring new costs that $1.50 doesn't capture.

options.text: Take what fits in the spare oven time, and price the rest separately
options.feedback: This treats the order as two different jobs with two different costs. The next card shows why that matters.

cards.title: One order, two very different halves.
body: The extra 100 loaves need an early-morning shift: $240 in overtime plus $30 of oven energy. That adds **$2.70 a loaf**. Taking the whole order earns $130 a day. Taking only the first half earns $200.

breakdown.label: First 100 loaves
breakdown.detail: $3.50 − $1.50 ingredients. Oven and staff are already paid.

cards.eyebrow: Concept at work · Fixed vs variable costs
cards.title: The $5.50 is mostly money she spends anyway.
body: Of the $5.50, only $1.50 rises with each loaf. That is the **variable cost**. The other $4.00 is her **fixed costs**, rent, oven and regular wages, spread over 300 loaves.
Spreading fixed costs is useful for setting shop prices. It misleads you on an extra order. Saying yes or no to the supermarket doesn't change the rent by a cent.

image.label: A loaf split into a small $1.50 slice and a large $4.00 slice
image.brief: 빵 한 덩이를 두 조각으로 자른 그림. 작은 조각 "Changes with each loaf $1.50", 큰 조각 "Paid anyway: rent, oven, wages $4.00". 큰 조각은 회색으로 흐리게 처리.

cards.title: The next loaf doesn't always cost the same.
body: **Marginal cost** is what one more unit adds to your total costs. While the oven has spare room, Mina's is $1.50.
Once the oven is full, the next loaf drags a whole extra shift with it. Her marginal cost jumps to $4.20. Costs often move in steps like this: flat until you hit capacity, then a sudden climb.

image.label: Step chart: cost per extra loaf jumps at 400 loaves
image.brief: 계단형 그래프. 가로축 "Loaves per day", 세로축 "Cost of the next loaf". 400개까지 $1.50로 평평하다가 400개에서 $4.20으로 뛰어오름. 400 지점에 "Oven full" 표시.

cards.softwareNote: Software has the same steps. Extra users cost almost nothing until a server tier, support team or database limit fills up. Then the next customer carries a big new cost.

cards.title: Mina wants to quote the second 100 loaves.
body: She'll happily take the first 100 at $3.50. What price should she ask for the 100 that need the early shift?

options.text: $3.50, the same as the first 100, to keep it simple
options.feedback: Simple, but each of those loaves costs $4.20 to make. She'd be paying $70 a day for the privilege of working longer.

options.text: $4.20, exactly what each extra loaf costs
options.feedback: No loss, but no gain either. She takes on an early shift and more risk for nothing.

options.text: Above $4.20, say $4.80, or delivery on days the oven has room
options.feedback: Pricing against marginal cost makes the second half pay its own way: $60 a day more, for $260 in total.

cards.title: Cheap today can get expensive later.
body: Ignoring fixed costs works for spare capacity. If the order grows and Mina must buy a second oven or rent more space, those new fixed costs belong to this order, and $3.50 may not cover them.
Watch your own shop too. If regulars start buying her bread at the supermarket, each lost $6 shop sale costs her $4.50. One wholesale loaf at $3.50 earns only $2.00.

cards.title: Now it's a delivery company.
body: Your vans drive goods from the city to suburban stores each morning, then drive back empty. A wholesaler offers $60 a trip to carry stock back to the city.
Your accountant says a trip costs $180 once drivers, fuel and van leases are spread in. Loading the return cargo adds about $15.

options.text: Decline. $60 is a third of what a trip costs
options.feedback: The van makes the return trip anyway, with the driver already paid. Declining gives up about $45 a trip.

options.text: Accept on return trips, and charge more for any extra trips
options.feedback: Return trips use spare capacity, so the marginal cost is $15. A dedicated trip adds around $120 in driver time and fuel, so $60 would lose money there.

options.text: Accept, and add extra trips at $60 if they want more
options.feedback: Same mistake as baking 400-plus loaves at $3.50. Beyond spare capacity, each extra trip costs more than it earns.

cards.title: Split a big order where your capacity runs out.
body: Price the part that fits in spare capacity against its true extra cost. Price the rest against the new costs it brings.
**Try it today:** find the point where your business runs out of room, whether ovens, vans, staff hours or servers. Write down what the next unit costs before and after that point.
list: **Fixed vs variable costs:** the $5.50 'cost' was mostly rent and wages paid anyway
**Marginal cost:** the next loaf cost $1.50, then $4.20 once the oven was full
